options.a: Deadlines are targets, and a party may perform within a reasonable time after
options.b: The closing date is binding, but contingency deadlines may be extended freely
options.c: The contract must close within 30 days of acceptance to remain enforceable
options.d: Contract dates and times are critical and late performance may be a breach

distractorExplanations.a: That is the reasonable-time standard that applies when the clause is absent; the clause makes dates strict.
distractorExplanations.b: The clause applies to all contract dates, including contingency deadlines, not just the closing date.
distractorExplanations.c: The clause enforces the dates the parties chose; it does not impose a fixed 30-day closing period.

options.a: A misstatement of a measurable fact, such as square footage, made without intent
options.b: A seller's silence about a known latent defect that a buyer could not discover
options.c: Exaggerated opinion that a reasonable person would not treat as a factual warranty
options.d: Advertising that omits the brokerage name, making it a blind ad under license law

distractorExplanations.a: A false measurable fact is negligent misrepresentation even without intent; puffing is only opinion or hype.
distractorExplanations.b: Silence about a known latent defect is concealment or nondisclosure, not exaggerated opinion.
distractorExplanations.d: That describes a blind ad, a license-law advertising violation unrelated to exaggerated sales talk.

options.a: Using client trust money for the broker's own business or personal expenses
options.b: Depositing several clients' earnest money deposits into one trust account
options.c: Mixing client trust money with personal or operating funds improperly
options.d: Holding earnest money beyond the deadline for depositing it into escrow

distractorExplanations.a: Spending trust money on the broker's own expenses is conversion, a separate and more serious violation.
distractorExplanations.b: Pooling multiple clients' funds in one properly kept trust account is permitted; mixing in broker money is not.
distractorExplanations.d: Late deposit is a timeliness violation of trust-account rules, not the mixing of trust and personal funds.

options.a: Inheritance
options.b: Homestead
options.c: Reversion
options.d: Survivorship

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses joint tenancy with tenancy in common; a joint tenant's interest passes to co-owners, not heirs.
distractorExplanations.b: Homestead is a separate protection of a residence from certain creditors, not a feature of joint tenancy.
distractorExplanations.c: Reversion is the grantor's future interest after a life estate, unrelated to co-ownership rights.

options.a: An FHA loan is used with a down payment of 3.5%
options.b: A VA loan is used with no down payment at all
options.c: Conventional LTV is high (commonly above 80%)
options.d: Conventional LTV falls to 78% of original value

distractorExplanations.a: FHA loans carry the government's mortgage insurance premium (MIP), not private mortgage insurance.
distractorExplanations.b: VA loans are guaranteed by the VA and do not require PMI even with no down payment; a funding fee applies instead.
distractorExplanations.d: 78% of original value is when borrower-paid PMI terminates under the Homeowners Protection Act, not when it starts.

options.a: Obtain the highest possible price even when the seller directs a quicker sale
options.b: Promote the seller's interests with loyalty, care, and obedience within the law
options.c: Treat buyer and seller with equal advocacy so both receive fair representation
options.d: Advise the seller on title and tax matters as the seller's legal representative

distractorExplanations.a: Price is not the top duty; obedience requires following the seller's lawful instruction to favor a quick sale.
distractorExplanations.c: Equal advocacy describes a neutral or dual role; a listing broker owes loyalty to the seller client, not both sides.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses agency with legal practice; a broker must refer title and tax questions to an attorney or CPA.

options.a: The seller's reasons for selling and the lowest price the seller is willing to accept
options.b: The racial or religious makeup of the neighborhood surrounding the property
options.c: That a former occupant of the home was living with HIV or AIDS
options.d: Known latent defects or conditions that could significantly affect value or desirability

distractorExplanations.a: Seller motivation and bottom-line price are confidential client information, not material property facts.
distractorExplanations.b: Discussing neighborhood racial or religious composition is steering under the Fair Housing Act, not a required disclosure.
distractorExplanations.c: HIV/AIDS is a protected disability under federal fair housing law; it is not a material property fact to disclose.

co-real-estate-readiness-check-agency-la.explanation: Material property defects and legally required disclosures must be shared; confidential motivations may be protected. Disclosure duties follow applicable law.

options.a: Proceed as a dual agent after giving the buyer written notice of the relationship
options.b: Switch to representing the buyer while keeping the seller's listing active for both
options.c: Terminate the listing agreement unilaterally and refund the seller's marketing costs
options.d: Not create the dual agency relationship; consider designated agency, referral, or withdrawal

distractorExplanations.a: Dual agency requires informed consent from both parties; notice to the buyer alone cannot replace the seller's consent.
distractorExplanations.b: Representing the buyer while still holding the listing is undisclosed dual agency, the exact thing the seller refused.
distractorExplanations.c: Refusing dual agency does not let the broker abandon the listing; the broker simply declines to represent the buyer.

options.a: Upon the death of the remainderman
options.b: When the life tenant sells the estate
options.c: Upon the death of the original grantor
options.d: Upon the death of the measuring life

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the remainderman with the measuring life; if the remainderman dies first, the remainder passes to his heirs and the life estate continues.
distractorExplanations.b: A life tenant may convey the interest, but the buyer simply holds a life estate pur autre vie that still ends at the original tenant's death.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the grantor with the measuring life; the grantor's death does not end an estate measured by the life tenant's life.

co-real-estate-readiness-check-property-.explanation: Life estates are measured by a life; the estate ends when the measuring life dies (or as otherwise defined in the grant), and the remainder or reversion follows.

options.a: Buy and sell existing mortgages, improving liquidity
options.b: Originate new loans directly to borrowers at closing
options.c: Insure lenders against borrower default on high-LTV loans
options.d: Set the discount rate that member banks pay the Fed

distractorExplanations.b: That describes the primary mortgage market, where lenders originate loans; the secondary market buys loans already made.
distractorExplanations.c: That is the role of private mortgage insurance or FHA insurance, not the secondary market's buying and selling of loans.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the secondary market with the Federal Reserve, which sets the discount rate as a monetary-policy tool.

co-real-estate-readiness-check-finance-c.explanation: Entities like Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac (and others) buy existing loans, improving liquidity for originators so they can lend again.

options.a: Fund construction in stages as work is completed, then convert to a permanent loan
options.b: Finance a short-term gap, often between purchase of a new home and sale of an existing one
options.c: Let the buyer take over the seller's existing mortgage at its original interest rate
options.d: Combine several parcels under one mortgage with partial releases as lots are sold

distractorExplanations.a: That describes a construction (construction-to-permanent) loan with draws, not short-term bridge or swing financing.
distractorExplanations.c: That describes a loan assumption, where the buyer takes over the seller's existing note, not a bridge loan.
distractorExplanations.d: That describes a blanket mortgage with a partial release clause, typically used by developers, not a bridge loan.

options.a: Within 10 days after the offer is accepted, using the closing disclosure packet
options.b: After both parties sign the purchase contract, as part of the closing documents
options.c: Before or as soon as practicable when the dual/designated relationship arises
options.d: Only if one party asks, since customers are not owed agency disclosures

distractorExplanations.a: Disclosure after acceptance is too late; the 10-day closing-packet timing confuses closing paperwork with relationship disclosure.
distractorExplanations.b: Waits until contract signing; the dual/designated relationship must be disclosed when it arises, before parties rely on it.
distractorExplanations.d: Disclosure is a licensee duty, not on request; customers are still owed brokerage relationship disclosure.

options.a: The listing broker is owed a commission if the property sells during the term, regardless of who finds the buyer
options.b: The listing broker is the sole agent, but the seller owes no commission on a buyer the seller finds personally
options.c: Any broker who procures the buyer earns the commission, and the seller may list with other firms at the same time
options.d: The listing broker keeps any sale proceeds above the seller's stated net price, whoever finds the buyer

distractorExplanations.b: That describes an exclusive agency listing, where the owner's own sale earns no commission.
distractorExplanations.c: That describes an open listing, where only the procuring broker is paid and multiple firms may list.
distractorExplanations.d: That describes a net listing (compensation above a net figure), not an exclusive right-to-sell agreement.

options.a: Give the buyer a recommended offer price, since customers are owed the same advice
options.b: Avoid acting as the buyer's advocate and stay within the listing agency role
options.c: Tell the buyer the seller's bottom line, since honesty duties run to the buyer too
options.d: Refuse to give the buyer any property facts until the buyer signs an agency agreement

distractorExplanations.a: Customers are owed honesty and material facts, not advocacy; recommending an offer price is buyer advocacy against the seller.
distractorExplanations.c: The seller's lowest acceptable price is confidential; honesty to the buyer does not override the listing client's confidentiality.
distractorExplanations.d: Material property facts must be disclosed to customers too; the limit is on advocacy, not on sharing facts.

co-real-estate-readiness-check-agency-la.explanation: Listing agents represent the seller; advocacy for a buyer requires a proper agency shift/disclosure. If the firm's policy allows it, buyer agency must be properly created and disclosed before advising the buyer.

options.a: Was induced by fraud or was a minor
options.b: Accepted the offer orally rather than in writing
options.c: Signed a purchase contract that was not notarized
options.d: Changed their mind before the closing date

distractorExplanations.b: An oral real estate contract is unenforceable under the statute of frauds, which is different from voidable by a protected party.
distractorExplanations.c: Notarization is not required for a purchase contract to be valid; it matters for recording deeds, not voidability.
distractorExplanations.d: Buyer's or seller's remorse does not make a contract voidable; that would be a breach unless a contingency applies.

options.a: The broker's fee is a fixed percentage set by the state real estate commission, removing price negotiation
options.b: The listing has no expiration date, so the seller cannot end the agreement if the broker fails to market it
options.c: The broker's compensation is the amount above a seller's net price, creating conflict-of-interest concerns
options.d: The broker's compensation is a flat fee that ignores the sale price, removing any incentive to market well

distractorExplanations.a: Commission rates are negotiable and are not set by any commission; fixing them would raise antitrust issues, not net-listing issues.
distractorExplanations.b: A missing expiration date is a separate listing-agreement defect; net listings are risky because of how the broker is paid.
distractorExplanations.d: Describes a flat-fee listing; in a net listing the broker keeps the excess over the seller's net, which is the conflict.

options.a: A right to purchase on stated terms within a period, usually for consideration
options.b: A right to match any third-party offer if the owner later decides to sell
options.c: An obligation to buy on stated terms once the optionor accepts the deposit
options.d: Equitable title and possession from the date the option is signed

distractorExplanations.b: That is a right of first refusal, which depends on a third-party offer; an option sets the purchase terms up front.
distractorExplanations.c: An option binds only the optionor; the optionee has a right, not an obligation, to buy.
distractorExplanations.d: Equitable title arises under a purchase contract or land contract; an unexercised option gives neither title nor possession.

options.a: Practicing law whenever they fill in names, prices, and dates on a standard form
options.b: Required to have an attorney sign the form before it can be presented
options.c: Exempt from unauthorized-practice rules once the client initials each page
options.d: Practicing law if they draft novel legal clauses beyond authorized forms

distractorExplanations.a: Filling in factual blanks on approved forms is permitted; unauthorized practice begins with drafting new legal clauses.
distractorExplanations.b: No attorney signature is needed before presenting an approved form; attorney review, where it exists, happens after signing.
distractorExplanations.c: Client initials do not authorize a licensee to draft legal language; unauthorized-practice limits still apply.

options.a: Public use and payment of the assessed tax value
options.b: Public use/purpose and just compensation
options.c: Owner consent and a negotiated sale price
options.d: An owner dying without heirs or a will

distractorExplanations.a: Just compensation means fair market value, not the property tax assessed value.
distractorExplanations.c: Condemnation works without the owner's consent; a negotiated voluntary sale is not eminent domain.
distractorExplanations.d: That is escheat, where property passes to the state; eminent domain is a taking from a living owner for public use.

options.a: A zoning violation that blocks issuance of a building permit
options.b: An unpaid utility bill owed by the current occupant
options.c: A quitclaim deed used to transfer title between spouses
options.d: A claim, encumbrance, or defect that may impair marketability

distractorExplanations.a: Zoning violations are land-use problems; a cloud on title is a claim or defect affecting ownership.
distractorExplanations.b: An occupant's personal debt is not a claim against title unless it becomes a recorded lien.
distractorExplanations.c: A quitclaim deed is a valid conveyance form; using one does not by itself create a cloud on title.

options.a: Must acquire title at the same time through the same deed
options.b: May hold unequal shares and typically lack survivorship unless specified
options.c: Must hold equal shares but may convey them without the others' consent
options.d: Pass their shares to the surviving co-owners rather than to their heirs

distractorExplanations.a: Unity of time and title is a joint tenancy requirement; tenants in common may acquire at different times.
distractorExplanations.c: Equal shares are a joint tenancy requirement; tenants in common may hold unequal shares.
distractorExplanations.d: Survivorship is the hallmark of joint tenancy; a tenant in common's share passes to heirs or devisees.

options.a: Permanent change of the zoning map for an entire district
options.b: Permission to deviate from a zoning requirement due to hardship
options.c: Permission to continue a use that predates the current zoning rules
options.d: Approval of a use the ordinance permits subject to a hearing and conditions

distractorExplanations.c: That describes a nonconforming use (grandfathered use), not a variance granted for hardship.
distractorExplanations.d: That is a special or conditional use permit; a variance relieves a hardship from a specific requirement.
distractorExplanations.a: That is rezoning/amendment.

co-real-estate-readiness-check-property-.explanation: Variances grant relief from strict zoning application in hardship cases. The zoning board or other zoning authority grants it.

options.a: Recording the deed in the public land records
options.b: Notarizing the grantor's signature on the deed
options.c: Delivering the signed deed to the grantee at closing
options.d: Purchasing an owner's title insurance policy

distractorExplanations.b: Acknowledgment makes a deed eligible for recording, but notice to the world comes from recording itself.
distractorExplanations.c: Delivery and acceptance transfer title between the parties but do not give constructive notice to third parties.
distractorExplanations.d: Title insurance indemnifies the owner against title defects; it does not put the public on notice of the deed.

options.a: Land bordering a lake, sea, or ocean shoreline
options.b: Land bordering flowing water such as a river or stream
options.c: Rights to minerals beneath the surface of the land
options.d: Water rights won by first beneficial use (prior appropriation)

distractorExplanations.a: Rights along lakes, seas, and oceans are littoral rights; riparian rights concern flowing water.
distractorExplanations.c: Subsurface mineral rights are a separate bundle of rights, unrelated to rights along a watercourse.
distractorExplanations.d: Prior appropriation (first in time, first in right) is a different water doctrine from riparian rights tied to bordering land.

options.a: Down payment ÷ purchase price × 100%
options.b: Total monthly debt ÷ gross monthly income × 100%
options.c: Appraised value ÷ loan amount × 100%
options.d: Loan amount ÷ appraised value × 100%

distractorExplanations.a: That gives the down payment percentage, the complement of LTV, not the loan-to-value ratio itself.
distractorExplanations.b: That is the back-end debt-to-income ratio, a borrower qualifying measure, not loan-to-value.
distractorExplanations.c: Inverts the ratio; LTV puts the loan amount on top and the property value underneath.

co-real-estate-readiness-check-finance-c.explanation: LTV ratios loan size to property value. Many lenders use the lower of appraised value or purchase price.

options.a: 1% of the purchase price
options.b: 1% of the loan amount
options.c: 1% of the down payment
options.d: 1% of the appraised value

distractorExplanations.a: Points are based on the loan amount, not the purchase price; the two differ by the down payment.
distractorExplanations.c: The down payment is the buyer's equity, not the borrowed amount on which points are calculated.
distractorExplanations.d: Appraised value is used for LTV, not for pricing points; a point is 1% of the loan amount.

options.a: Both interest and principal so the balance declines over the term
options.b: Interest only for the term, with principal due as a balloon at maturity
options.c: Principal and interest, with the payment amount rising each year
options.d: Mostly principal early, with the interest share growing over the term

distractorExplanations.b: That describes an interest-only loan with a balloon payment, not an amortizing loan.
distractorExplanations.c: A fixed-rate amortizing payment stays level for principal and interest; rising payments describe a graduated-payment loan.
distractorExplanations.d: Reverses amortization: early payments are mostly interest, and the principal share grows over time.

options.a: Banning certain kickbacks and requiring settlement cost disclosures
options.b: Requiring lenders to disclose APR and finance charges on consumer credit
options.c: Banning lending discrimination based on race, sex, or marital status
options.d: Requiring lenders to report mortgage application data by census tract

distractorExplanations.b: APR and finance-charge disclosure comes from the Truth in Lending Act (Regulation Z), not RESPA.
distractorExplanations.c: That is the Equal Credit Opportunity Act; RESPA targets settlement kickbacks and cost disclosures.
distractorExplanations.d: Census-tract application reporting is the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act (HMDA), not RESPA.

options.a: Charges a fee when a monthly payment arrives after the grace period ends
options.b: Lets the lender demand the full balance when the borrower sells the property
options.c: Requires extra payment if the borrower pays off early, when the note allows it
options.d: Lets the lender call the entire balance due after the borrower misses a payment

distractorExplanations.a: That is a late-charge clause; a prepayment penalty applies to paying the loan off early.
distractorExplanations.b: That is an alienation (due-on-sale) clause, triggered by transfer, not a prepayment charge.
distractorExplanations.d: That is an acceleration clause triggered by default; a prepayment penalty is triggered by early payoff.

options.a: Adjusts to the current prime rate at every monthly payment
options.b: Can adjust based on an index plus margin, subject to caps
options.c: Changes only when the borrower refinances into a new loan
options.d: Adjusts based on the lender's margin alone, with no rate caps

distractorExplanations.a: ARMs adjust at set intervals using a chosen index plus margin; no rule ties them to prime monthly.
distractorExplanations.c: Describes a fixed-rate loan replaced by refinancing; an ARM rate adjusts within the same loan.
distractorExplanations.d: The margin is fixed; adjustments follow the index, and most ARMs carry periodic and lifetime caps.

options.a: Lender losses if the borrower defaults with less than 20% equity
options.b: Fire and storm damage to the structure during ownership
options.c: Covered title defects and claims against ownership per the policy
options.d: Defects in title arising after the policy date, like new liens

distractorExplanations.a: That is private mortgage insurance (PMI), which covers credit risk, not title defects.
distractorExplanations.b: Casualty losses are covered by hazard or flood insurance, not by a title policy.
distractorExplanations.d: Title insurance covers defects existing as of the policy date; liens created later are excluded.

options.a: The lender pays the item outside of closing
options.b: The buyer is charged; it increases cash needed
options.c: The seller is charged and the buyer is credited the same amount
options.d: The buyer receives a credit reducing cash to close

distractorExplanations.a: Items paid outside closing (POC) are shown for disclosure but are not a debit charged to the buyer.
distractorExplanations.c: Reverses the entry; a buyer debit charges the buyer, while a seller debit with buyer credit is a different proration entry.
distractorExplanations.d: That describes a credit.

co-real-estate-readiness-check-finance-c.explanation: Debits charge a party; buyer debits typically increase funds due at closing. A seller debit works the same way and reduces the seller's proceeds.

options.a: Maximum loan amounts that lenders may make to one borrower
options.b: Maximum interest rates that may be charged on certain loans
options.c: Minimum down payments required on certain home loans
options.d: Disclosure of the annual percentage rate on consumer loans

distractorExplanations.a: Loan-size limits (such as conforming loan limits) are separate; usury caps the interest rate.
distractorExplanations.c: Down payment minimums are set by loan programs and lenders, not by usury statutes.
distractorExplanations.d: APR disclosure is a Truth in Lending requirement; usury laws limit the rate itself.

options.a: Covers the broker's intentional misrepresentations to buyers
options.b: Replaces the duty to disclose known material defects
options.c: Protects buyers against defects in the title to the property
options.d: May be required, but does not excuse license law violations

distractorExplanations.a: E&O policies exclude intentional or fraudulent acts; they cover negligent errors.
distractorExplanations.b: Insurance coverage does not replace disclosure duties; nondisclosure remains a license violation.
distractorExplanations.c: That describes title insurance; E&O covers the licensee's professional negligence.

options.a: Illegal only if the buyer files a HUD complaint within one year
options.b: Allowed if the seller gives the instruction in writing before the showing
options.c: Illegal under federal fair housing law and also violates license standards
options.d: Allowed under the single-family owner exemption even when a broker lists it

distractorExplanations.a: The one-year limit is a HUD complaint filing deadline; the refusal is illegal whether or not a complaint is filed.
distractorExplanations.b: A written seller instruction cannot legalize discrimination; licensees must refuse it in any form.
distractorExplanations.d: The owner's single-family exemption is lost once a broker or licensee is used to sell or rent.

options.a: Lets the broker delegate legal responsibility for supervision to team leaders
options.b: Shields the managing broker from discipline for an agent's violations
options.c: Satisfies the licensees' continuing education requirement once they read and sign it
options.d: Documents supervision standards and compliant procedures for affiliated licensees

distractorExplanations.a: Tasks may be delegated, but the employing or managing broker stays legally responsible for supervision.
distractorExplanations.b: A manual supports supervision but does not shield a broker who fails to supervise in practice.
distractorExplanations.c: Continuing education must come from approved courses; reading a firm manual does not count.

options.a: License discipline and civil claims
options.b: Civil claims against the seller alone
options.c: Discipline only after a lawsuit
options.d: No liability under an as-is clause

distractorExplanations.b: The licensee who knew of the defect is also exposed to civil liability, not just the seller.
distractorExplanations.c: The commission can discipline on a complaint alone; no prior lawsuit or judgment is required.
distractorExplanations.d: An as-is clause does not protect a licensee who conceals a known material defect.

options.a: Held by the listing agent personally until both parties sign the contract
options.b: Forwarded to the buyer's lender and held there until final loan approval is issued
options.c: Deposited into a properly designated trust/escrow account within required timelines
options.d: Kept in the operating account, with a ledger entry identifying the client

distractorExplanations.a: Agents may not personally hold trust funds; they go to the brokerage's trust account on the required timeline.
distractorExplanations.b: The lender is not the earnest money holder; funds go to the designated trust or escrow account.
distractorExplanations.d: A ledger entry does not cure commingling; client money must be in a separate trust account.

options.a: Depends on education/exam waivers and any required state-portion steps
options.b: Is handled by ARELLO, which issues licenses valid in member states
options.c: Lets the licensee practice in Colorado on the home-state license alone
options.d: Requires retaking both the national and state exams in every case

distractorExplanations.b: ARELLO is an association of regulators; it issues no licenses, and each state commission decides recognition.
distractorExplanations.c: A home-state license does not authorize Colorado brokerage activity; a Colorado license is required.
distractorExplanations.d: Licensed out-of-state applicants usually have the national portion waived and take the state portion.

options.a: Moves with the associate, who becomes responsible for the records
options.b: Remains with the brokerage; the firm retains responsibility for records
options.c: Is split so the associate keeps open files and the firm keeps closed ones
options.d: Goes to the state commission, which holds records for the retention period

distractorExplanations.a: Transaction records belong to the brokerage; the departing associate does not take custody or responsibility.
distractorExplanations.c: Open and closed files both remain with the brokerage; listings and records belong to the firm.
distractorExplanations.d: The commission audits records but does not store them; the brokerage must retain them.

options.a: Allowed in print but not on social media
options.b: Allowed if the ad includes the agent's cell phone number
options.c: Prohibited or restricted by advertising rules
options.d: Allowed for private-party listings the agent owns personally

distractorExplanations.a: Advertising identification rules apply to every medium, including print and online ads.
distractorExplanations.b: A phone number does not identify the licensee status or brokerage; the firm name is still required.
distractorExplanations.d: A licensee selling their own property must still disclose licensee status in the ad.

options.a: May negotiate repairs and price terms if the supervising broker approves each offer
options.b: Must hold a broker license to schedule inspections and appraisals and track contract deadlines
options.c: Performs administrative tasks under supervision and must not negotiate unless licensed
options.d: Takes over supervision duties when the managing broker is unavailable

distractorExplanations.a: Negotiating terms is licensed activity; broker approval does not let an unlicensed coordinator negotiate.
distractorExplanations.b: Scheduling and deadline tracking are administrative tasks that do not require any license.
distractorExplanations.d: Supervision belongs to a licensed broker; an unlicensed coordinator cannot stand in for one.

options.a: Allowed for any active licensee, since REALTOR® is a generic license title
options.b: Allowed if the licensee belongs to a local MLS but not the association
options.c: A matter for the association alone, with no advertising-law consequences
options.d: Improper trademark/membership misuse and can also be deceptive advertising

distractorExplanations.a: REALTOR® is a registered membership mark of NAR, not a license title any licensee may use.
distractorExplanations.b: MLS access does not confer association membership; the mark requires REALTOR® association membership.
distractorExplanations.c: Misusing the mark is also misleading advertising that the state commission can discipline.
